english: doing one thing and then switching mid-action (and in the middle...)
formNote: Attach -다가 straight onto any verb stem with no sound change (가다 → 가다가, 먹다 → 먹다가, 일하다 → 일하다가). The picture is: you were in the middle of action 1, and before finishing it you stopped, switched, or something else happened — so action 1 is left unfinished, often interrupted by surprise. In casual speech the 가 is dropped to just -다 (집에 가다 길 잃었어). CONTRAST with -고 나서: -다가 means the first action was cut short partway (밥 먹다가 나갔어 = stopped eating, left), whereas -고 나서 means it fully finished first (밥 먹고 나서 나갔어 = ate, then left). Also note 같은 주어 — the doer of action 1 and action 2 is normally the same person. Pitfall for English speakers: 'while' in English covers both simultaneous and interrupted action, but if two things truly happen AT THE SAME TIME with no switch (listen to music while studying), that is -(으)면서, not -다가.
usage: Frozen adverbial: a switch or event happens mid-trip
I woke up in the middle of sleeping
at this rate / if this keeps up
Set phrase warning of a bad outcome ahead
examples: 집에 가다가 편의점 들렀어요.
On my way home I stopped by the convenience store.
Simple: 가다가 = en route, then a detour. 들르다 = drop by
넷플릭스 보다가 그냥 잠들어 버렸어.
I was watching Netflix and just ended up falling asleep.
Casual; pairs naturally with -아/어 버리다 for an unintended result
걸어가다가 옛날 회사 동료를 만났어요.
I ran into an old work colleague while walking.
Real situation: an unexpected event cuts into the ongoing action; 동료 = coworker
mistakes: Using -다가 for an action you fully finished first — if you finished eating and then left, that is 밥 먹고 나서 나갔어요, not 밥 먹다가 나갔어요 (which means you abandoned the meal halfway).

Using -다가 for two genuinely simultaneous actions with no switch — 'I study while listening to music' is 음악 들으면서 공부해요 (-(으)면서), because nothing is interrupted or switched; -다가 needs a mid-action change.
Adding past tense to the first verb when you mean a simple switch — say 보다가 잤어요, not 봤다가 잤어요. (보았다가-type forms exist but flip the meaning to 'did and then undid,' a different nuance.)

english: after finishing (and then, once that's done)
formNote: Attach -고 나서 to any verb stem with no sound change (먹다 → 먹고 나서, 끝나다 → 끝나고 나서, 운동하다 → 운동하고 나서). The 나다 part ('to come out / be completed') adds the feeling that action 1 is thoroughly DONE and over before action 2 starts — it stresses completion more strongly than plain -고. CONTRAST with plain -고: 손 씻고 먹어요 just lists two actions in order, but 손 씻고 나서 먹어요 spotlights 'only after the washing is fully finished do I eat.' CONTRAST with -은 후에/-은 다음에: those are interchangeable in meaning ('after'), but -고 나서 sounds more spoken and a touch more emphatic about finishing. You can swap to -고 나면 for a conditional 'once you've done X, then...' (운동하고 나면 개운해요). Pitfall: only the FINAL verb carries tense — never put -았/었 on the first clause (밥 먹고 나서, not 밥 먹었고 나서), and the subject of both clauses is normally the same person.
usage: First action fully completed before the next
I work out after I get off work
Common with 보다 'try'; decide only once you've mulled it
examples: 손 씻고 나서 밥 먹어요.
Wash your hands and then eat.
Simple and emphatic: eat only once the washing is done
월급 받고 나서 한턱낼게요.
Once I get my paycheck, I'll treat you.
Everyday: 한턱내다 = treat someone; the treat waits on the payday being complete
회의 끝나고 나서 같이 점심 먹어요.
Let's have lunch together after the meeting wraps up.
Office sequence; tense sits only on the final verb 먹어요, not on 끝나다
mistakes: Adding tense to the first clause — it's 밥 먹고 나서, not 밥 먹었고 나서. Only the final verb shows tense.
Forcing -고 나서 onto adjectives or 있다 — you cannot say 예쁘고 나서 or 있고 나서; this pattern is for completed ACTIONS only, so use a different connector for states.
Reaching for -고 나서 when you just want a plain 'and' list of two actions — 청소하고 빨래했어요 (did the cleaning and the laundry) needs only -고; add 나서 only to spotlight that the first is fully finished first.

english: while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)
formNote: Add -ㄴ 채로 to vowel-ending stems (켜다 → 켠 채로) and -은 채로 to consonant-ending stems (입다 → 입은 채로, 앉다 → 앉은 채로). 채 is a noun meaning 'the state as it stands,' so the structure literally says 'in the state of having done X.' It describes doing the main action while a PRIOR state is left unchanged — you turned the light on, then left it that way and slept. The 로 is often dropped to just -(으)ㄴ 채. CONTRAST with -(으)면서: -(으)면서 is two ACTIONS at once (먹으면서 봐요 = eat while watching, both ongoing), but -(으)ㄴ 채로 freezes a finished state that simply persists (불 켠 채로 잤어요 = the turning-on already happened, the lit state just remains). CONTRAST with -(으)ㄴ 상태로, which is almost identical but a touch more neutral/written; -채로 carries a faint nuance of 'and you weren't supposed to.' Pitfall: pick verbs that leave a lasting result-state (켜다, 신다, 앉다, 누르다, 열다), never an ongoing motion — 'while running' is not 뛴 채로 but 뛰면서.
usage: I slept with the light left on
A finished state (lit) held during sleeping
He came in with his shoes still on
신다 → 신은 채로; a big faux pas in Korean homes
서다 → 선 채로; the standing state held during eating
감다 → 감은 채로; common set image
examples: 양말 신은 채로 슬리퍼 신었어요.
I put slippers on over my socks (with my socks still on).
Simple result-state: the socks were already on and stayed on. 신다 → 신은 채로
어제 화장 안 지운 채로 그냥 잤어요.
I just slept last night without taking my makeup off.
Everyday confession; note 안 ... -ㄴ 채로 = 'without having done X.' 화장 지우다 = remove makeup
에어컨 켠 채로 외출하면 전기세 많이 나와요.
If you go out with the AC left on, the electric bill runs high.
Real living tip; the AC's on-state persists while you're out. 전기세 = electricity bill
mistakes: Using it with an ongoing action to mean 'while doing' — 'while eating' is 먹으면서, not 먹은 채로. -(으)ㄴ 채로 needs a held STATE (앉은 채로 = while seated), not a continuing action.
Using the wrong tense ending — it's always -(으)ㄴ 채로 (the result-state form), never 켜는 채로 or 켤 채로; the state must already exist before the main clause happens.
Negating in the wrong spot — to say 'without taking it off,' put 안 before the verb: 안 벗은 채로, not 벗지 않은 채로 ... 안. The 안 ... -(으)ㄴ 채로 frame is the natural one.

english: because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)
formNote: Attach -는 바람에 to any verb stem (늦다 → 늦는 바람에, 놓치다 → 놓치는 바람에, 막히다 → 막히는 바람에). 바람 here is not 'wind' the weather but a noun meaning 'a sudden gust of cause/consequence,' so it frames an abrupt, unintended reason that led to a negative or surprising result. Despite the present-looking -는, it always points to a PAST cause, and the result clause sits in past tense. Because the cause is outside your control, it commonly comes off as an excuse. CONTRAST with -아서/어서: -아서 is the neutral all-purpose 'because' (good or bad, 길이 막혀서 늦었어요 just states it), while -는 바람에 adds the flavor 'and that unwelcome thing ruined it' (길이 막히는 바람에 = traffic, of all things, jammed me up). CONTRAST sharply with -덕분에 'thanks to,' which is the POSITIVE cause for a good result. Pitfall: it takes verbs only, never adjectives (no 추운 바람에), and you cannot use it for a command or suggestion in the result clause.
usage: The classic 'it wasn't my fault' excuse setup
I was late because of traffic
막히다 = get jammed; cause beyond your control
Unintended cause leading to a bad result
갑자기 pairs well; an out-of-the-blue disruption
examples: 늦잠 자는 바람에 버스를 놓쳤어요.
I overslept and so I missed the bus.
Simple cause→bad result; the result clause 놓쳤어요 is past
앞에서 사고가 나는 바람에 두 시간이나 갇혔어.
There was an accident up ahead so I was stuck for two whole hours.
Casual; 사고(가) 나다 = an accident happens, 갇히다 = get stuck. 이나 stresses the painful amount
서버가 터지는 바람에 작업을 처음부터 다시 했어요.
The server crashed so I had to redo the work from scratch.
Office/tech real situation; 서버(가) 터지다 = the server blows up/crashes
mistakes: Using it for a good result — 바람에 carries a disruptive, unwelcome nuance, so for a welcome cause use -아서/어서 or -덕분에 (thanks to): 친구 덕분에 잘 끝났어요, never 친구가 도와주는 바람에 잘 끝났어요.
Attaching it to an adjective — there is no 추운 바람에 or 바쁜 바람에; the cause must be a verb (an event), so rephrase as 날씨가 추워서 or use a verb like 추워지는 바람에.
Putting the result clause in present/future or as a command — 늦는 바람에 빨리 가세요 is wrong; the result of a 바람에 cause is a past fact (늦었어요), not an instruction.

english: it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)
formNote: Add -ㄹ 텐데 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 올 텐데, 바쁘다 → 바쁠 텐데) and -을 텐데 to consonant-ending stems (좋다 → 좋을 텐데; 힘들다 drops ㄹ → 힘들 텐데). It comes from 터(예정·추측의 의존명사, 'the expected case') + -ㄴ데, so it means 'it must/should be the case that...' followed by a contrast, worry, or gentle suggestion. For a PAST guess use -았/었을 텐데 (피곤했을 텐데 = you must have been tired). It often trails off softly as a caring -ㄹ 텐데(요). CONTRAST with -ㄹ 건데, which sounds nearly the same but means 'I'm GOING to (my own plan), but' (저는 갈 건데 = I intend to go) — 텐데 is a GUESS about someone/something, not your own intention. CONTRAST with -겠지만: that is a drier 'probably... but,' while -ㄹ 텐데 leans warm and considerate, anticipating the listener's situation. Pitfall: English 'would' is ambiguous; here it is conjecture about a likely state, so don't use it for plans or promises.
usage: Considerate lead-in before asking a favor
you must be worn out, so rest a bit
you must be hungry, so eat something
they should be here soon, but...
Assumption that often leads into puzzlement
examples: 지금쯤 도착했을 텐데 연락이 없네요.
They should've arrived by now, but there's no word.
Simple past guess -았/었을 텐데 + a worried contrast
주말이라 사람 많을 텐데 예약하고 가자.
It's the weekend so it'll probably be packed — let's book and go.
Casual planning: a guess (많을 텐데) leads to a sensible suggestion
월세도 빠듯할 텐데 너무 무리하지 마세요.
Money must be tight with rent, so don't overdo it.
Considerate real-life advice; 월세 = monthly rent, 빠듯하다 = be tight
mistakes: Confusing it with -ㄹ 건데 (a plan: 'I'm going to, but') — 내일 비가 올 텐데 is a GUESS about the weather, while 내일 갈 건데 is YOUR intention to go. Mixing them flips a forecast into a plan.
Using it for a fact you already know for certain — if you've confirmed they arrived, say 도착했는데, not 도착했을 텐데; 텐데 is specifically for an unconfirmed conjecture.
Forgetting the past form for a past guess — 'you must have been tired yesterday' is 어제 피곤했을 텐데, not 어제 피곤할 텐데, which would point the guess at the wrong time.

english: (I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)
formNote: Attach -더니 directly to a verb or adjective stem (그러다 → 그러더니, 아프다 → 아프더니, 기침하다 → 기침하더니). The 더 is the 'I personally witnessed it' retrospective marker, so -더니 links something you SAW/HEARD firsthand in the past to the result or change that followed — 'he kept coughing (I watched it), and then he got sick.' The subject of plain -더니 is normally someone/something OTHER than 'I,' because you're reporting an outside observation. CONTRAST with -았/었더니: that combined form flips the subject to 'I' and means 'because I did/experienced X, this resulted' (많이 먹었더니 배불러 = I ate a lot, so now I'm full); use 었더니 for your own cause, plain 더니 for what you observed in others. CONTRAST with -니까: -니까 is a neutral logical 'because/since,' while -더니 always carries that eyewitness, watched-it-unfold flavor and a sense of change. Pitfall: don't narrate your own neutral actions with plain -더니 — it sounds odd to say 내가 가더니.
usage: Links an observed action to what followed next
he kept coughing and then caught a cold
it was cold this morning but now it's warm
I ate a lot so now I'm sleepy
examples: 하늘이 어둡더니 비가 오네요.
The sky got dark and now it's raining.
Simple observed cause→change; 더니 reports what you watched happen
걔 어제 야식 먹더니 오늘 속이 안 좋대.
She had a late-night snack yesterday and now says her stomach's off.
Casual; subject is 걔 (someone else), 야식 = late-night food
하루 종일 굶었더니 머리가 어지러워요.
I starved all day so now I feel dizzy.
Here -았더니 = MY own action led to this state; 굶다 = skip meals
mistakes: Using plain -더니 about your OWN action — for 'I overdid it, so...' say 내가 무리했더니, not 내가 무리하더니. Plain -더니 is for what you observed in someone/something else.

Mistaking -더니 for a neutral 'because' like -니까 — 비가 오니까 우산 챙겨 (since it's raining, take an umbrella) is logical reasoning, but 비가 오더니 길이 막히네 means 'it started raining and then, sure enough, the road jammed' — eyewitness change, not a request.
Pairing -더니 with a command or suggestion in the second clause — say what RESULTED (감기 걸렸어요), not an instruction; 기침하더니 약 먹어 is wrong.

english: since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)
formNote: Attach -길래 directly to a verb or adjective stem (싸다 → 싸길래, 울다 → 울길래, 맛있다 → 맛있길래); for nouns use N(이)길래. It gives a reason rooted in something you personally NOTICED or were told, which then prompted your own response — so the second clause is almost always YOUR own choice, usually past tense (싸길래 샀어요 = it was cheap, so I bought it). CONTRAST with -아서/어서: -아서 states a general or objective cause for any result (싸서 잘 팔려요 = it's cheap so it sells well, a fact about the world), but -길래 ties an observed reason specifically to what YOU then did in reaction. CONTRAST with -기에: same meaning, but -기에 is the more formal/written twin, while -길래 is conversational and warmer. Pitfall: the result clause cannot be a general truth or someone else's action — 'it's cheap so everyone buys it' is 싸서 다들 사요, not -길래; -길래 must lead to your own reactive deed. It also doesn't fit commands ('since it's cheap, buy it' uses 싸니까, not 싸길래).
usage: it was cheap so I bought it
it looked good so I ordered it
there was no reply so I called
everyone was going so I went too
examples: 맛있어 보이길래 하나 샀어요.
It looked tasty so I bought one.
Simple: observed reason (looked good) → my action (bought)
편의점에서 1+1 하길래 두 개 사 왔어요.
It was buy-one-get-one at the convenience store so I grabbed two.
Everyday deal; 1+1 (원 플러스 원) = BOGO; reason I saw → what I did
리뷰가 좋길래 그 식당을 예약했어요.
The reviews were good so I booked that restaurant.
Real decision based on info; 리뷰가 좋다 = reviews are good → my booking
mistakes: Using -길래 when the second clause isn't your own reactive action — 'it's cheap so it sells well' is a general fact (싸서 잘 팔려요), not 싸길래 잘 팔려요. -길래 leads to what YOU did in response.
Using -길래 in a command or request — 'since it's cheap, buy it' is 싸니까 사 or 싸길래 사긴 어렵다... no; use 싸니까 사세요. The result of -길래 is a past deed you already did, not an order to someone.

Putting it with your own internal reason rather than an observed one — 'I was hungry so I ate' is best as 배가 고파서 먹었어요; -길래 wants an external trigger you noticed (others, a sign, a price), not your own feeling.

english: (it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)
formNote: Add -ㄴ 지 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 온 지, 만나다 → 만난 지) and -은 지 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹은 지; 살다 drops ㄹ → 산 지). It measures the time ELAPSED since an action happened, and is normally followed by a duration plus 됐어요/지났어요 (한국에 온 지 1년 됐어요 = it's been a year since I came to Korea). Crucially, write 지 with a SPACE — this time-elapsed 지 is a separate noun-like word. CONTRAST sharply with the negative-ish -지 in 안/-지 않다: 온 지 1년 됐어요 (space; time since) vs 오지 않았어요 (no space; 'didn't come') are completely different 지. CONTRAST also with -(으)ㄴ 후에 'after': 온 후에 = once you've arrived (sequence), but 온 지 = how much time has passed since arriving (measurement) — they are not interchangeable. Pitfall: only works with verbs (an action that started the clock), never adjectives; ask elapsed time with 얼마나 됐어요? ('how long has it been?').
usage: it hasn't been long since I came
it's been a year since we met
Duration + 되다 to clock the gap
it's been a while since I ate
how long since you bought it?
사다 → 산 지; asking elapsed time
examples: 밥 먹은 지 한 시간밖에 안 됐어요.
It's only been an hour since I ate.
Simple measurement; 밖에 + 안 = 'only.' Note 먹다 → 먹은 지
한국에 산 지 이제 막 6개월 됐어요.
I've only just hit six months living in Korea.
Newcomer self-intro; the ㄹ-drop 살다 → 산 지 is the tricky part
걔랑 연락 끊은 지 진짜 오래됐어.
It's been ages since I cut off contact with them.
Casual; 연락(을) 끊다 = stop contact → 끊은 지 measures the gap
mistakes: Forgetting the space and confusing it with negative -지 — '온 지 1년' (space, time elapsed) vs '오지 않았어요' (no space, negation). They are different 지 entirely.
Using the present or future form of the verb — it must be the past-attributive -(으)ㄴ (온 지, 산 지), never 오는 지 or 올 지, because the action that started the clock is already done.
Mixing it up with -(으)ㄴ 후에 'after' — 졸업한 후에 취직했어요 (after graduating I got a job, a sequence) is not 졸업한 지 취직했어요; use 지 only to count how long it's been (졸업한 지 3년 됐어요).

english: the more (you do/it is) X, the more Y
formNote: Add -ㄹ수록 to vowel-ending stems (가다 → 갈수록, 보다 → 볼수록) and -을수록 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을수록; 알다 drops ㄹ → 알수록). It expresses proportional change: as one thing increases, another shifts along with it ('the more X, the more Y'). It is very commonly reinforced by putting -(으)면 on the front of the same verb — 보면 볼수록 (the more I look), 알면 알수록 (the more I learn) — a fixed, natural-sounding doubling. Write 수록 ATTACHED to the stem with no space. CONTRAST with -(으)니까/-아서 'because': those give a single cause→effect, but -ㄹ수록 sets up a sliding scale where Y keeps moving as X keeps growing. Pitfall: don't write a space (-ㄹ 수록 is wrong) and don't confuse it with the ability pattern -ㄹ 수 있다 — 갈수록 (more and more, one chunk) has nothing to do with 갈 수 있다 (can go). English 'the more... the more' uses two clauses with 'the'; Korean folds it into one suffix, so resist translating word for word.
usage: more and more (as time goes on)
Frozen adverbial; things intensify over time
the more I look, the prettier it is
면 + 수록 doubling for natural emphasis
the more I eat, the sleepier I get
the more I learn, the harder it gets
examples: 보면 볼수록 좋아져요.
The more I see it, the more I like it.
Simple set phrase; the 면+수록 doubling is how natives say it
한국어는 하면 할수록 재밌는 거 같아요.
The more I do Korean, the more fun it seems to get.
Encouraging learner line; 하다 → 할수록
서울은 살수록 정이 드는 도시예요.
Seoul is a city you grow more attached to the longer you live there.
정(이) 들다 = grow attached; 살다 → 살수록 (ㄹ-drop)
mistakes: Writing a space (-ㄹ 수록) or confusing it with -ㄹ 수 있다 — 수록 is one chunk attached to the stem (갈수록), unrelated to the ability 수 있다.
Dropping the helpful -(으)면 lead-in where natives expect it — 'the more I look' sounds bare as just 볼수록; the idiomatic form is 보면 볼수록 with the verb repeated.
Forgetting the ㄹ-irregular drop — 알다 becomes 알수록 (not 알을수록) and 살다 becomes 살수록 (not 살을수록); the stem ㄹ stays and you add just 수록.

english: even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)
formNote: Attach -더라도 directly to a verb or adjective stem (가다 → 가더라도, 힘들다 → 힘들더라도, 늦다 → 늦더라도); for nouns N(이)더라도. It concedes a strong or even unlikely hypothetical — 'even supposing that happens, the result still holds.' For a past supposition use -았/었더라도 (알았더라도 = even if I had known). It very often pairs with 아무리 ('no matter how') up front for extra force. CONTRAST with -아도/어도: both translate as 'even if,' but -아도 is the everyday, can-be-real concession (비가 와도 가요 = even if it rains I'll go, quite plausible), while -더라도 is stronger and more hypothetical, used for emphatic or less likely cases (비가 오더라도 = even supposing it rains). CONTRAST with -(으)ㄴ/는데도 'even though,' which concedes a REAL current fact (비가 오는데도 = even though it IS raining), not a hypothetical. Pitfall: don't reach for -더라도 to describe something already happening — that's -는데도; reserve -더라도 for suppositions, especially after 아무리.
usage: no matter how busy, eat your meals
I'll go even if it rains
come for sure even if you're late
examples: 조금 비싸더라도 좋은 걸로 살래요.
Even if it's a bit pricey, I'll buy the good one.
Simple concession; 더라도 grants the price point and holds the choice
아무리 피곤하더라도 운동은 빠지지 마.
No matter how tired you are, don't skip your workout.
Casual firm advice; 아무리...더라도 is the natural pairing
조건이 좋더라도 계약서는 꼼꼼히 봐요.
Even if the terms look good, read the contract carefully.
Practical living advice; 계약서 = contract, 꼼꼼히 = thoroughly
mistakes: Treating it as identical to -아도/어도 — both mean 'even if,' but -더라도 is more hypothetical and emphatic, used for stronger or less likely suppositions, while -아도 fits ordinary, plausible cases.
Using -더라도 for a fact that is actually true right now — 'even though it's raining (and it is)' is 비가 오는데도, not 비가 오더라도, which only supposes the rain.
Forgetting the past form for a past hypothetical — 'even if I had known' is 알았더라도, not 알더라도, which would wrongly point the supposition at the present.
